Power, phasors and complex power

Why this matters in the exam: Question 1 of the exam (20 marks) is “AC and DC Power Circuit Analysis”, and it is built almost entirely from Chapters 1–2. In June 2023, Q1a (battery model, 5 marks) and Q1c (series RLC phasors and , 9 marks) were pure M1 material. In June 2024, Q1a(ii), Q1b and Q1c (efficiency, a motor’s pf and from and , and series RL and , about 9 marks) were too. The rest of Q1 is power-factor correction and star/delta, which are covered in pack M2 and use exactly the same tools. The 2023 quiz (Q1–Q2, 12 of 40 marks) and the 2024 test (Q1–Q3, 16 of 40 marks) follow the same pattern. Expect 10–14 of the 20 marks in Q1 to come from this pack.

1. The core ideas

Course conventions (use these exactly)

  • Subscript 1 means a phase quantity (, ), and subscript L means a line quantity.
  • All AC magnitudes are rms. Mains “240 V” means V and V.
  • The voltage is the phase reference: , .
  • is the angle of the current relative to the voltage. Lagging (inductive) means . Leading (capacitive) means .
  • The power triangle angle is , so . This is why an inductive load (with ) gives .
  • Always quote the power factor with its label, e.g. “0.8184 lag”.

Equivalent circuits (Section 1.1, 2.1)

A real source or load is replaced by ideal elements you can analyse. For a DC source (a battery or power supply), the model is an EMF in series with an internal resistance .

Test What it gives Formula
Open circuit () the EMF
Loaded, with and measured the internal resistance
Short circuit the internal resistance
Any load the terminal voltage
Maximum power occurs when , at 50 % efficiency

Trap: the power delivered to the load is (using the terminal voltage), not . is the total, and it includes the loss.

Mechanical power and speed (Section 1.4)

  • Use this whenever a question gives torque and speed. That is: motor output power, or generator input power.
  • Quick check: the speed in rpm is about 10 times the speed in rad/s (1500 rpm = 157.1 rad/s).
  • Trap: putting rpm straight into gives an answer about 10 times too large.

Efficiency (Section 1.7)

  • Motor: is electrical and is mechanical. Generator: the reverse.
  • A motor’s rating (“1.1 kW motor”) is its output (mechanical) power.
  • Any two of , , and give the other two.

Single-phase AC power (Section 1.5)

  • is the average of . Its maximum is and its minimum is , where . The minimum is negative whenever : energy then flows back to the source for part of each cycle.
  • To get a phase shift from a time delay: . If the current peaks earlier than the voltage, it is leading.
  • In a balanced three-phase system, the total instantaneous power is constant. This means less vibration. It is a common short-answer point.

Drag φ from lagging to leading and watch p(t) dip below zero whenever Q ≠ 0, while the shaded average P = V₁I₁cos φ shrinks.

Three-phase power (Section 1.6, brief; details are in M2)

  • Nameplate values are line voltage, line current and total power. If the connection is not stated, assume star: and .
  • The pf of a balanced 3ph load equals the pf of one phase.

Complex power and the power triangle (Section 2.4)

  • Units: in VA, in W, in VAr.
  • The conjugate is essential. without the gives the wrong angle.
  • and are each conserved. The total is the sum of the element ’s, and the same holds for . is not: never add apparent powers. Add the ’s, add the ’s, and then recombine.
  • When you get , take the sign from the physics: inductive or lagging gives , and capacitive or leading gives .
  • Power-factor correction (M2): a parallel capacitor supplies negative . This reduces the supply , and current, and leaves unchanged. That is the whole idea; the method is in M2.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Leaving out the conjugate. . Without the , the sign of flips, as does the lead/lag label you derive from it.
  • rpm in . Always convert with first. If comes out larger than , you forgot this step.
  • Adding magnitudes. and . Add phasors, or add and separately.
  • Using the wrong formula for the topology. works for series, and works for parallel. Practice Question 2.17(f) asks why fails for the parallel case: the line current does not flow through the resistor.
  • Unlabelled pf, or a sign error on . Write “0.8184 lag”, not “0.8184”. For lagging, is negative, so the current phasor has a negative angle.
  • Peak vs rms. Machines quantities are rms. Use peak only when the question asks for the waveform amplitude ().
  • The calculator atan quadrant. For , the angle is , not .
  • Three-phase line vs phase. Using overstates by . Use , or .

Power Circuit Tool WS1 Q1 (workshop). Time-Domain Waveforms: Using the default values of load P = 100 W and Q = 100 VAr, examine the equations for and which are given just above the voltage and current time waveforms.

  1. What are the peak and rms values of the voltage and current waveforms?
  2. For each of the values of Q = 100 VAr, 0 VAr and −100 VAr: (i) indicate whether the current is leading, lagging or in-phase; (ii) indicate whether the power factor is leading, lagging or unity.
Solution

Hint: W, VAr, V.

  1. The tool shows , so 240 V and 339.4 V. VA, so 0.589 A and 0.833 A.

  2. VAr: the current lags and the pf is lagging (inductive load absorbs Q). : the current is in phase and the pf is unity. VAr: the current leads and the pf is leading (capacitive load generates Q).

These match the official answers.

Power Circuit Tool WS1 Q2 (workshop). Phasors: examine the relationship between the phasor graph and the time-domain graphs.

  1. Which direction are the phasors rotating?
  2. Does the x-axis or y-axis component of the phasors correspond to the instantaneous voltage and currents? You may find it convenient to use the animation control buttons: start, stop, step and reset/zero.
  3. Reset the phasors to stop them rotating. As you change Q = 100 VAr, 0 VAr and −100 VAr, how do you work out whether the current is leading, lagging or in-phase with the voltage?
Solution

  1. Anticlockwise (the standard direction for phasors, at rad/s).

  2. The y-axis component. The tool’s waveforms are written with , so the vertical projection of each rotating phasor gives the instantaneous value.

  3. With as the reference at , look at the angle of the current phasor. Below the voltage phasor (clockwise from it, e.g.  for VAr) means lagging. On top of it means in phase. Above it (anticlockwise, for VAr) means leading.

(ii) What is the (approx.) minimum value of the instantaneous power? Note that negative values of instantaneous power are associated with reactive power. We will cover this in the next workshop.

  2. Whenever or .

(c)(i) No change. The average stays at W for all three values of Q.

  1. , so its minimum is . For : VA and the minimum is 0 W. For VAr: VA and the minimum is −41.4 W. The official sheet reads about −41.2 W off the graph, so the difference is only graph-reading accuracy.

Jun24 Q1a(ii) (past exam, 2 marks). Fill-In-The Blank. An electric motor has an input power of 1000 W and a power loss of 300 W. This results in an output power of ______ W and an efficiency of ______ %. Increasing the power loss for the same input power would cause the efficiency to ______ (choose decrease or increase). Increasing the input power for the same power loss would cause the efficiency to ______ (choose decrease or increase).

Solution

700 W and 70 %. More loss for the same input means decreases. More input for the same loss means increases, because the loss becomes a smaller fraction of the input.

These match the official answers.

Jun24 Q1b (past exam, 3 marks). Electrical and Mechanical Power. Consider a 3ph, 4 pole, 50 Hz induction motor. Under a certain operating condition, the motor speed is 1420 rpm, input voltage is 415 V, input current is 6.8 A, input electrical power is 4 kW and output torque is 23 Nm.

  1. Find its input power factor (you can assume this is lagging). [1 mark]
  2. Find its output power and hence efficiency. [2 marks]
Solution

Hint: Playbook B. A 3ph nameplate gives line values.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

M1  POWER, PHASORS, COMPLEX POWER  (rms throughout; V1 = V1/_0 is the reference)
phi = angle of I relative to V.  lag (inductive): phi<0, Q>0.  lead (capacitive): phi>0, Q<0
w = 2*pi*n/60 [rad/s]   (rpm ~ 10 x rad/s)    P_M = τ*w    τ = F*r, F = m*g
eta = Pout/Pin   Ploss = Pin - Pout = Pin(1-eta)   motor: Pin electrical, Pout = τ*w
     motor rating = OUTPUT (shaft) power; 3ph nameplate = line V, line I, total P; assume star
DC source:  E = Voc,  Rs = (E - V)/I,  V = E - I*Rs,  Pload = V*I,  Pmax at RL = Rs
1ph: P = V1 I1 cos(phi)   Q = V1 I1 sin(-phi)   S = V1 I1     Vpk = sqrt2 * Vrms
3ph: S = 3 V1 I1 = sqrt3 VL IL,  P = sqrt3 VL IL cos(phi),  pf(3ph) = pf(1 phase)
p(t) = P + S cos(2wt + phi):  average P, freq 2f, min = P - S (negative if Q != 0)
|phi| = (dt / T) * 360 deg; current peaks earlier => leading
Z:  R,  jwL,  -j/(wC).   Series: add Z.  Parallel: Z1Z2/(Z1+Z2) or add branch currents
S = V1 * conj(I1) = P + jQ = S/_(-phi)    pf = P/S = cos(phi)  (STATE lead/lag)
Q = +/- sqrt(S^2 - P^2): sign from physics (L +, C -)
Sum P's and sum Q's over loads; never sum S's.
SERIES RL (same I):   V1^2 = VR^2 + VL^2,  R = P/I^2,  X = Q/I^2,  P:Q = R:X
PARALLEL RL (same V): I1^2 = IR^2 + IL^2,  R = V^2/P,  X = V^2/Q,  P:Q = X:R
L = X/w    C = 1/(w|X|)    series RLC: |VL| or |VC| may exceed V1; f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC))
Check every answer:  P = sum I^2 R  and  Q = sum I^2 X (signed)
Calculator: if Re < 0, add/subtract 180 deg to the atan result
PF correction (see M2): a parallel C makes Q negative; P is unchanged; supply S and I fall
